newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel ignites talk of reshuffle in Kohl's cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Waigel ignites talk of reshuffle in Kohl's cabinet.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl should replace several ministers before launching the 1998 election campaign, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in interviews on Sunday which quickly ignited speculation of a cabinet reshuffle.

With surprising candour, Waigel said in a series of interviews that a number of ministers were only trying to hang on to their jobs until the election, and urged Kohl to jettison any who were tiring well before the 1998 campaign starts.
"In the fall, if there are a number of ministers who no longer have the desire, then the chancellor should form a new team," Waigel told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
In another interview with Der Spiegel news weekly, Waigel was even blunter, saying there was no room in the cabinet for anyone who was merely marking time until the next election.
"If there is a minister or two wanting to leave but eager to hang on until the election, one should tell him 'Comrade, it would be nice, but we have to form our new team now'."

The remarks from Waigel, a loyal ally of Kohl, came less than one month after Kohl abruptly stamped out speculation of a cabinet reshuffle by saying he saw no reason to make changes before the next election.

But with opinion polls showing the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) slumping behind the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), Waigel's coordinated campaign had all the markings of an attack at least tacitly endorsed by Kohl.
Guido Westerwelle, the general secretary of Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), said he was also in favour of making changes before the election rather than after.
"I personally have a lot of sympathy for Theo Waigel's view," Westerwelle told a rally in the eastern town of Doebeln.
FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhardt often speaks out against any changes, even though he is rumoured to be in line for the job of economics minister.
Despite occasional rumours of cabinet changes during the first three years of Kohl's fourth term, there have be no changes in the 17-member cabinet since it took office in November 1994.

Waigel declined to say which ministers he was referring to, but the Christian Social Union (CSU) party chairman is widely reported to have his eye on the foreign ministry, now held by Klaus Kinkel of the FDP.
Waigel fuelled that speculation by telling the Leipziger Volkszeitung newspaper that if he were no longer finance minister he would like to work on parliament's foreign affairs committee.
The Bild am Sonntag weekly identified Interior Minister Manfred Kanther of the CDU and Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt of the FDP as likely targets of his broadside.

Rexrodt, who is often called ineffective by politicians in the CDU as well as his own FDP, has staved off several attempts to force him out in the last few years. The newspaper said CDU leaders believe Kanther has failed to give his office enough profile.
Labour Minister Norbert Bluem (CDU), who turns 63 in 1998, was also thought to be on the hit list, Bild am Sonntag said.

"One year before the election the chancellor has to have the right to shape the cabinet so that those who stay and the new arrivals will be available to remain in the cabinet for a full four years after the elections," Waigel told the Leipziger Volkszeitung.
